rows.label: HFHI's US advocacy cost booked in its US affiliates programme, FY2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: The Form 990 describes Habitat Voices in Action and HFHI's advocacy grants to affiliates under the US programme's heading (Part III line 4B; Schedule C: grants 'to support coalition building, grassroots building, and advocacy'), and the public awareness programme (line 4C) as media and events, so part of the advocacy's cost is in the US affiliates line. HFHI's whole lobbying spending was $877,000 (Schedule C); with policy staff, advocacy grants and campaign tools, about $2 million, range $1 million to $4 million. Taken out of the US model's cost and put in the awareness model's, so each counts it once.

rows.label: HFHI's Home Equals cost booked in its international programme, FY2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: The Form 990 reports Home Equals under 'Global impact' (line 4A, the international programme), so part of its cost (global policy staff, area offices' advocacy, campaign grants to national organisations) is in that line: about $1.5 million, range $0.5 million to $3 million. Taken out of the international model's cost and put in the awareness model's.

rows.label: Spillovers of Habitat's housing work in low- and middle-income countries, as a share of the families' consumption value
rows.explainer: Local builders, masons and material sellers earn from the work, and upgraded drainage, water and paths serve neighbours, as neighbours gain from cash transfers' spending (GiveWell's adjusted Egger et al. 2022 spillover is about 0.7 for cash in Kenya). Housing money buys more imported or factory goods (cement, roofing sheets) than cash does, and the evidence for construction is weaker, so 0.1, range 0 to 0.4. Read by the international model's direct branch and the awareness model's Home Equals branch; not by market purchases, which are trades, not new spending.

rows.label: Deaths averted by Habitat's housing work in low- and middle-income countries, as a share of the families' consumption value
rows.explainer: Deaths only: cement floors, latrines, drainage and improved stoves cut children's diarrhoea and respiratory illness (Piso Firme, Cattaneo et al. 2009, measured illness, not deaths), so some child deaths are averted where that is the work. GiveWell's mortality effect for cash is about 0.2 of consumption value; floors, latrines and stoves are a small part of Habitat's housing work, so 0.03, range 0 to 0.1; times your value of a life. Illness itself is in each model's unmodelled_benefits_adj. Read by the international model's direct branch and the awareness model's Home Equals branch.

rows.label: Volunteers across the Habitat network, worldwide, FY2025

source.title: Habitat for Humanity International, Form 990 for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, Schedule O
source.quote: THE NUMBER OF VOLUNTEERS REPORTED BY ALL HABITAT FOR HUMANITY INTERNATIONAL, INC. (HFHI) ENTITIES IN FY25 WAS 828,000.

rows.explainer: Everyone who volunteered with HFHI, an affiliate or a national organisation in the year, worldwide (the annual report gives 827,607). Their time isn't in any financial statement, so the US and international models add it as a resource behind the homes, each its own share.

rows.label: Share of the Habitat network's volunteers working on US homes and repairs
rows.explainer: No split of Habitat's volunteers by country or activity is published. Most Habitat volunteering is on US build and repair sites (corporate, church and student build days); Global Village trips and national organisations' volunteers abroad are a minority, and a share of US volunteers work in the 863 ReStores, which sell donated goods to fund the affiliates and are not part of the homes' resources (like the donated goods themselves). 0.5 of the network's volunteers on US homes and repairs, range 0.3 to 0.75.
